Females of Neoscorpis lithophilus reach a moderate maximum size, with an ultimate total length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm] attained by the largest individuals in sampled populations. This asymptotic length, derived from extensive field surveys along the subtropical coastline of southern Africa, places the stone-bream among the larger-bodied species within its family, the Kyphosidae. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a predictable power-law trajectory, and based on the 30 cm [Lp = 30 cm] fork length at which females typically attain puberty, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 464 grams [Wwp = 464 grams]. This mass threshold marks a significant physiological transition, as reproductive maturation in Neoscorpis lithophilus is believed to be closely tied to the acquisition of sufficient somatic reserves to support vitellogenesis and subsequent spawning events. The fork length at puberty represents a critical life-history parameter for fisheries management, given that size-selective harvesting of individuals below this value could substantially reduce the reproductive potential of the stock. Comparative data from related kyphosids suggest that the length at maturity observed in South African waters is consistent with regional patterns for warm-temperate reef fishes.

The early life stages of Neoscorpis lithophilus begin with remarkably small offspring. The wet weight at birth, calculated from the mean egg diameter reported for this species, is approximately 0.000523 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000523 grams], a value that reflects the pelagic, yolk-dependent larval phase characteristic of the family. Newly hatched prolarvae emerge from transparent, buoyant eggs that measure between 0.9 and 1.4 mm in diameter, and the initial mass of each hatchling is derived from the volumetric formula for a sphere, assuming a density equivalent to that of seawater. This tiny birth mass imposes a tight energetic constraint on the subsequent larval period, during which the yolk-sac larva must absorb its endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The rapid depletion of lipid stores during the first few days post-eclosion dictates a critical window for prey detection and capture; failure to initiate first feeding within this period leads to irreversible starvation and mortality. Field observations of larval dispersal along the Agulhas Current suggest that the pelagic larval duration may span several weeks, during which growth is exponential under favorable thermal regimes.

As females approach the terminal phase of their growth trajectory, the ultimate wet weight recorded for the species reaches 2158 grams [Wwi = 2158 grams]. This maximum body mass, corresponding to the upper bound of the length-weight relationship for the population, is typically achieved by the largest, oldest individuals inhabiting structurally complex reef habitats. The relationship between length and weight in Neoscorpis lithophilus conforms closely to a cubic function, and the predicted ultimate weight derived from the ultimate length of 50 cm aligns well with empirical records from commercial and recreational catches. Attaining this asymptotic mass requires an extended period of somatic investment, during which the energetic surplus beyond maintenance and activity costs is directed primarily toward tissue accretion. Comparative analyses of kyphosid body composition indicate that the ultimate wet weight of stone-bream is intermediate between that of the smaller, more abundant species within the genus and the larger, more offshore-oriented congeners. This size ceiling likely reflects a combination of resource availability, metabolic constraints imposed by the local thermal environment, and the energetic demands of annual reproductive cycles.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Neoscorpis lithophilus is approximately 4% [GSI = approximately 4%] under thermal conditions of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Gonadal recrudescence in this species is initiated during the early spring, with vitellogenesis proceeding as water temperatures rise, and the peak of the spawning season coincides with the warmest months of the year.

The maximum lifespan documented for Neoscorpis lithophilus is approximately 4015 days [am = approximately 4015 days] based on recapture data from tagged individuals and validated by otolith microchemistry, at an average environmental temperature of 21.9 °C [T = 21.9 °C]. This longevity places the stone-bream among the longer-lived members of the Kyphosidae, a family generally characterized by moderate to extended lifespans. The age estimates were derived from annual growth increment counts in sagittal otoliths and corroborated by mark-recapture records spanning more than a decade in the iSimangaliso Wetland Park. Individuals inhabiting warmer, more productive inshore reefs tend to reach asymptotic size more rapidly but may experience slightly reduced lifespans compared to those in cooler offshore environments, suggesting a trade-off between growth rate and longevity. The oldest recorded specimen, a female corresponding to the maximum length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], showed no signs of reproductive senescence, indicating that stone-bream maintain fecundity throughout their adult lives. This extended reproductive window, combined with iteroparous spawning, buffers the population against recruitment failures in years of unfavorable oceanographic conditions.
